Prealgebra · Lesson 6.5

Inequalities

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Every equation so far had one exact answer, the number that makes both sides match. Many questions are not like that. A recipe wants the oven at least 350350 degrees, so 351351 and 400400 work too, and a bridge bars trucks above a posted height, so many heights pass. A statement that compares two amounts instead of setting them equal is an inequality, and its solution is a stretch of the number line. Every balance move from 6.1 through 6.4 works here. Only one rule is new. Multiplying or dividing by a negative flips the sign.

Problem
A solo ride only lets you board if your ticket count is strictly more than 55, written t>5t>5. The word strictly matters, because holding exactly 55 is not enough, you have to clear the line, not land on it. Five friends hold 33, 55, 77, 1212, and 5.55.5 tickets. How many of those counts satisfy t>5t>5? Type the single number.
Show a hint
  • The rule is t>5t>5. Go through the friends one at a time and ask whether each ticket count is bigger than 55. Watch the friend holding exactly 55, since >5>5 does not include 55 itself.
  • Mark each value yes or no for t>5t>5. 33 is no, 55 is no because it only ties the line, 77 is yes, 1212 is yes, and 5.55.5 is yes. Count the yeses.
Show the full solution
Check each count against t>5t>5. 33 is no, 55 is no because it only ties the line, 77 is yes, 1212 is yes, and 5.55.5 is yes. That is 33​ friends. Strict means the boundary is out, so holding exactly 55 tickets fails even though it reaches the number.
Key idea
What an inequality says, and how to read it. An equals sign says both sides are the same number, so there is one answer. An inequality says only that one side is bigger than the other, so a whole band of numbers can make it true at once. Keep four symbols straight. The >> and << are strict, meaning the two sides can never be equal, while ≥≥ and ≤≤ allow the boundary value itself. On the number line the answer is a ray, not a dot. A hollow circle at the end means the endpoint is left out (strict >> or <<), a filled circle means it is included (≥≥ or ≤≤), and the arrow covers every value that works in that direction.
Problem
A delivery cart already holds 88 crates, and the running total must stay under 2020, so with xx more crates the rule is x+8<20x+8<20. Solve it the same way as x+8=20x+8=20, by subtracting 88 from both sides, with no sign flip for subtraction. The boundary is strict, so a value sitting exactly on it does not count. What is the largest whole number xx can be?
Show a hint
  • Make the first move you would make for an equation. Subtract 88 from both sides to get xx alone. Adding or subtracting the same amount never flips an inequality, so the << sign stays pointing the same way. Then notice the bound is strict, which matters for a whole number answer.
  • Subtracting 88 from both sides gives x<12x<12. Since xx must be strictly less than 1212, the value 1212 itself is out. The largest whole number that still fits is the integer just below 1212.
Show the full solution
Subtract 88 from both sides of x+8<20x+8<20 to get x<12x<12. Subtracting never flips the sign. The bound is strict, so 1212 is out and the largest whole number that fits is 1111​. Check it, 11+8=1911+8=19 which is under 2020, while 12+8=2012+8=20 is not.
Problem
A diver's gauge reads negatively below the surface. Her reading is xx, she rises 55 meters to x+5x+5, and the safety check needs the new reading at least 22, so x+5≥2x+5≥2. Subtract 55 from both sides, and subtracting never flips the sign. Because the sign is ≥≥, the boundary itself is allowed. What is the smallest value xx can be?
Show a hint
  • Treat the inequality just like an equation for the first move. To get xx by itself, undo the +5+5 by subtracting 5 from both sides. You only flip the inequality sign when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative, and subtracting does not do that, so the ≥≥ stays pointing the same way.
  • Subtract 5 from both sides of x+5≥2x+5≥2 and you get x≥−3x≥−3. The sign is ≥≥, which means −3−3 itself is allowed, so the gate is closed. The smallest reading that still works is the boundary number −3−3.
Show the full solution
Subtract 55 from both sides of x+5≥2x+5≥2 to get x≥−3x≥−3. Subtracting does not flip the sign. Because the sign is ≥≥, the boundary is allowed, so the smallest reading she can start from is −3−3​. The sign only reverses when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative, which never happens here.
Problem
Four identical sandbags sit on a shelf rated for at most 2626 kilograms total, so with one bag weighing xx, the rule is 4x≤264x≤26. Solve it like an equation, keeping the inequality sign. Divide both sides by the positive number 44, which does not flip the sign. The word most means the boundary counts. What is the largest value xx can be? Give a fraction in lowest terms.
Show a hint
  • The bags share the load, so undo the 44 by dividing both sides by 44. You are dividing by a positive number here, so watch what happens to the inequality sign. When you divide by a positive, the sign keeps pointing the same way, it does not flip.
  • Divide both sides of 4x≤264x≤26 by 44. The sign stays as ≤≤, giving x≤264x≤426​. Simplify 264426​ to lowest terms, and since the bound is "at most" the boundary itself is allowed, so the largest value is that boundary.
Show the full solution
Divide both sides of 4x≤264x≤26 by 44, a positive number, so the sign stays put. That gives x≤264x≤426​, which reduces to 132213​. At most means the boundary counts, so the heaviest one bag can be is 13/213/2​ kilograms. If the shelf were rated for under 2626 kilograms instead, 132213​ would be shut out and there would be no largest allowed weight.
Problem
Priya pays a flat $45$45 booth fee and clears $5$5 on each eraser she sells, so selling nn erasers gives a profit of 5n−455n−45 dollars. She wants that profit to be at least $200$200, so the goal is 5n−45≥2005n−45≥200. Solve it, dividing by the positive 55 without flipping the sign. What is the fewest whole erasers she must sell to reach her goal?
Show a hint
  • Each eraser adds 55 to her profit, but the 4545 booth fee gets subtracted once. Start by undoing that subtraction. Add 4545 to both sides so the nn term sits alone, and notice you are only adding and dividing by positive numbers here, so the ≥≥ sign stays pointing the same way the whole time.
  • After adding 4545 you get 5n≥2455n≥245. Divide both sides by 55, a positive number, so no flip, and you land on n≥49n≥49. Since she cannot sell part of an eraser and 4949 is already a whole number that is allowed, the fewest is 4949 itself.
Show the full solution
Add 4545 to both sides of 5n−45≥2005n−45≥200 to get 5n≥2455n≥245, then divide by 55, a positive, so no flip. That gives n≥49n≥49, and 4949 is a whole number that is allowed, so she needs 4949​ erasers. At 4949 the profit is 245−45=200245−45=200 dollars, which counts because at least includes hitting the goal exactly.
Key idea
Solve it like an equation. Solving an inequality is the same work as solving an equation, just with a >> or << where the == used to be. Tidy each side, undo a plus with a minus, undo a times with a divide. Adding the same amount to both sides keeps the bigger side bigger, and so does multiplying both sides by the same positive amount. Neither move changes the sign. Only one move is different. Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the sign.
Fun fact
The symbols << and >> first appeared in Thomas Harriot's 1631 book. The wide end faces the larger value. The rounded cousins ≤≤ and ≥≥ were popularized by Pierre Bouguer in the 1700s.
Problem
Start from a statement nobody would argue with, 3<83<8. Now multiply both sides by −1−1, so the 33 becomes −3−3 and the 88 becomes −8−8. On a number line, the one farther left is the smaller, so −8−8 is now the smaller value. Of the two results −3−3 and −8−8, which one is the larger? Type that value.
Show a hint
  • Put −3−3 and −8−8 on a number line and remember the rule from earlier chapters. Farther to the left means smaller, farther to the right means larger. Watch what happened to the order. The statement started as 3<83<8, with the left number smaller, but after the move the smaller one is no longer on the left.
  • Mark both numbers. −8−8 is eight steps left of zero, and −3−3 is only three steps left of zero, so −3−3 sits to the RIGHT of −8−8. The number on the right is the larger one. That is −3−3.
Show the full solution
Multiplying 3<83<8 by −1−1 turns the sides into −3−3 and −8−8. On the number line −8−8 sits farther left, so it is the smaller one, and the larger of the two is −3−3​. Copying the old direction would give −3<−8−3<−8, which is false. That is why multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative flips the sign.
Key idea
Flip the sign on a negative. When you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, you must flip the inequality, so << becomes >>, ≤≤ becomes ≥≥, and the same the other way. Multiplying by a negative reverses which value is bigger, so the sign has to flip. Adding, subtracting, and multiplying by a positive leave the sign as it is. Before writing a final answer, check whether you multiplied or divided by a negative.
Problem
A freezer alarm trips whenever −5x−5x climbs above 1717, so the danger zone is −5x>17−5x>17. To free xx, divide both sides by −5−5, and dividing by a negative flips the >> to <<. What is the largest integer xx can be?
Show a hint
  • Get xx alone by dividing both sides by −5−5. The moment you divide by a negative number, something has to happen to the inequality sign. Decide what it becomes before you read off the answer.
  • Dividing by −5−5 flips >> into <<, so x<−175x<−517​, which is x<−3.4x<−3.4. The gate at −3.4−3.4 is open, so −3.4−3.4 itself is not allowed. Now name the largest integer that sits strictly to the left of −3.4−3.4 on the number line.
Show the full solution
Divide both sides of −5x>17−5x>17 by −5−5. The divisor is negative, so the sign flips and x<−175=−3.4x<−517​=−3.4. The bound is strict, and the largest integer sitting left of −3.4−3.4 is −4−4​. Check it, −5⋅(−4)=20>17−5⋅(−4)=20>17 is true, while −5⋅(−3)=15>17−5⋅(−3)=15>17 is false.
Problem
This one pulls everything together. The variable appears on both sides and there is a group to clear. Solve 3(2−x)>2x+13(2−x)>2x+1 by distributing, then gathering the variable, and stay alert because one step divides by a negative and forces the sign to flip. Once you have the range, what is the largest integer xx can be?
Show a hint
  • Start exactly the way you would for an equation. Distribute the 33 across the parentheses to get 6−3x6−3x on the left, then move the variable terms to one side and the numbers to the other. Keep one eye out for a moment where you divide by a negative, since that is the only thing here that behaves differently from an equation.
  • After distributing you have 6−3x>2x+16−3x>2x+1. Subtract 2x2x from both sides to reach 6−5x>16−5x>1, then subtract 66 to get −5x>−5−5x>−5. Now divide both sides by −5−5, and because that divisor is negative, FLIP the sign. That gives x<1x<1. The bound is strict, so 11 itself is not allowed. Name the largest whole number that still sits below 11.
Show the full solution
Distribute the 33, so 3(2−x)>2x+13(2−x)>2x+1 becomes 6−3x>2x+16−3x>2x+1. Subtract 2x2x to get 6−5x>16−5x>1, then subtract 66 to get −5x>−5−5x>−5. Dividing both sides by −5−5 flips the sign, leaving x<1x<1. The bound is strict, so the largest integer that fits is 00​. At x=1x=1 both sides equal 33, and 3>33>3 is false, which is exactly why 11 is shut out.
Problem
Three runners are scored so a bigger number means faster. The sheet gives two facts. Priya beat Quinn, P>QP>Q, and Quinn was at least as fast as Rafe, Q≥RQ≥R. A teammate scribbles five claims, P>RP>R, P≥RP≥R, P>QP>Q, Q>RQ>R, and R>PR>P. Using only the two facts and the way inequalities chain when they point the same way, how many of the five claims are forced to be true? Type the single count.
Show a hint
  • Line the two facts up so the arrows point the same way, P>Q≥RP>Q≥R. Anything you can read straight off this chain by following greater-than signs from left to right is forced. Watch the spot where QQ meets RR, because that link is ≥≥ and not a strict >>.
  • Forced because they read straight off the chain, P>QP>Q is given outright, P>RP>R jumps across the whole chain, and P≥RP≥R is a weaker true statement that P>RP>R already guarantees. Not forced, Q>RQ>R fails whenever Quinn and Rafe tie since that link is only ≥≥, and R>PR>P is actually backwards. Count the forced ones.
Show the full solution
Stack the two facts into one chain, P>Q≥RP>Q≥R. Reading across it, P>QP>Q is given outright, P>RP>R follows because the trip across the chain crosses a strict >>, and P≥RP≥R follows since it is a weaker claim than P>RP>R. The other two are not forced. Q>RQ>R fails if Quinn and Rafe tie, since that link is only ≥≥, and R>PR>P points backwards. That is 33​ forced claims. One strict link anywhere makes the whole chain strict, but a chain of all ≥≥ leaves ties possible.
Problem
A compound inequality traps the variable in the middle. Solve 1<5−2x≤111<5−2x≤11. Whatever you do, do it to all three parts at once so the middle stays fenced in on both sides, and remember that dividing by the negative coefficient flips both signs together. Once you have xx cornered, how many integers make the whole thing true? Type the single count.
Show a hint
  • Peel away the constant from all three parts first. Subtract 55 from the left, the middle, and the right, and you should land on −4<−2x≤6−4<−2x≤6. Now you have to divide every part by −2−2, and that negative is about to do something to the signs, so stay alert.
  • Dividing all three parts by −2−2 flips BOTH inequality signs, which gives 2>x≥−32>x≥−3. Read that the tidy way around and it says −3≤x<2−3≤x<2, closed at −3−3 and open at 22. Now just list the integers from −3−3 up to but not including 22 and count them.
Show the full solution
Subtract 55 from all three parts of 1<5−2x≤111<5−2x≤11 to get −4<−2x≤6−4<−2x≤6. Divide every part by −2−2, and since −2−2 is negative both signs flip, giving 2>x≥−32>x≥−3. Written small to large that is −3≤x<2−3≤x<2, so the integers are −3,−2,−1,0,1−3,−2,−1,0,1, which is 55​ of them. Dividing by a negative also swaps which end is the floor and which is the ceiling, so rewrite the range in increasing order before you count.
Key idea
Two bounds at once. A compound inequality like 4<x≤94<x≤9 sets two conditions at the same time, a lower bound and an upper bound. Its solution is a segment with both ends marked, not a ray that runs on forever. Solve it with the same balance work, except that every move now applies to the left, middle, and right together. Multiplying all three by a negative flips both signs. Chaining is a related move. When several comparisons all point the same direction, combine them into one statement and read across it. If a first amount is greater than a second and the second is at least as large as a third, the first is greater than the third. Watch the symbols. One strict >> anywhere keeps the two ends strictly apart, but a chain of ≥≥ does not force the ends to differ, since they might be equal.
Problem
The trickiest one, folding everything together. Solve 5−2x−8>4−x5−2x−8>4−x. The left side has two number pieces sitting apart, so tidy it first, then gather the variables. One move near the end forces the sign to turn around. Once you have the range, what is the largest integer xx can be?
Show a hint
  • Start by combining the two number terms on the left, since 5−85−8 is a single value. That turns the left side into −3−2x−3−2x. Then gather the variables on one side the same way you did when solving equations. Keep an eye out for the step that might flip the inequality.
  • After tidying you have −3−2x>4−x−3−2x>4−x. Add xx to both sides to get −3−x>4−3−x>4, then add 33 to both sides to get −x>7−x>7. Now multiply both sides by −1−1, and because the multiplier is negative you must reverse the sign, giving x<−7x<−7. The bound is strict, so −7−7 itself is not allowed. The largest integer that fits is the whole number just below −7−7.
Show the full solution
Combine the numbers on the left, 5−8=−35−8=−3, so the inequality reads −3−2x>4−x−3−2x>4−x. Add xx to both sides to get −3−x>4−3−x>4, then add 33 to get −x>7−x>7. Multiplying both sides by −1−1 flips the sign, leaving x<−7x<−7. The bound is strict, so the largest integer is −8−8​. A bare −x−x carries a negative coefficient, so clearing it flips the sign just like dividing by −5−5 would.
Problem
A metal sample starts at 2222 degrees Celsius and the cooler pulls it down 1.51.5 degrees per minute, so after mm minutes its temperature is 22−1.5m22−1.5m. It freezes only once that drops strictly below −8−8, so the condition is 22−1.5m<−822−1.5m<−8. Solve it, remembering that dividing by the negative coefficient flips the sign. What is the fewest whole minutes the lab must wait until it freezes?
Show a hint
  • Solve 22−1.5m<−822−1.5m<−8 just like a normal equation. Subtract 2222 from both sides to get −1.5m<−30−1.5m<−30. Now watch closely, because your next move divides both sides by a negative number, and that does something to the inequality sign.
  • Divide both sides by −1.5−1.5. Dividing by a negative flips the sign, so −1.5m<−30−1.5m<−30 turns into m>20m>20. The bound is strict, so m=20m=20 does not count. Check it. At 2020 minutes the temperature is exactly −8−8, which is not below the line yet, and at 2121 minutes it is −9.5−9.5, which finally is. So the answer is the first whole number bigger than 2020.
Show the full solution
Subtract 2222 from both sides of 22−1.5m<−822−1.5m<−8 to get −1.5m<−30−1.5m<−30. Divide by −1.5−1.5, and the negative divisor flips the sign, giving m>20m>20. The bound is strict, so the lab waits 2121​ minutes. At 2020 minutes the sample is at exactly −8−8, which is not yet below the line, and at 2121 minutes it is −9.5−9.5.

Practice these ideas

Practice
A rewards account stays open as long as its balance ww satisfies w≥−4w≥−4, since a small overdraft is forgiven. Five accounts have balances −6−6, −4−4, −3−3, 00, and 55. How many satisfy w≥−4w≥−4?
Show the solution
Check each balance against w≥−4w≥−4. −6−6 fails, −4−4 passes, and −3−3, 00, and 55 all pass. That is 44​ accounts. The equals half of ≥≥ is what saves the account sitting exactly at −4−4.
Practice
A scanner keeps a reading mm only when m<7m<7 and tosses anything that hits or passes the threshold, so the strict sign leaves the boundary 77 out. One shift gives 22, 77, 6.96.9, 88, and −1−1. How many readings does the scanner keep?
Show the solution
Test each reading against m<7m<7. 22 is kept, 77 is not since 7<77<7 is false, 6.96.9 is kept, 88 is not, and −1−1 is kept. That is 33​ readings. A strict less-than never lets a value equal the boundary, so the reading of exactly 77 goes out.
Practice
A ferry deck already holds 1313 crates, and loading xx more must keep the total under 2525, so x+13<25x+13<25. Solve it. What is the largest integer number of extra crates xx can be?
Show the solution
Subtract 1313 from both sides of x+13<25x+13<25 to get x<12x<12. Subtracting does not flip the sign. The bound is strict, so the largest whole number of extra crates is 1111​. Eleven brings the deck to 2424, while 1212 would hit 2525 exactly, which the rule does not allow.
Practice
A pilot's dial setting xx must satisfy x−9≥−2x−9≥−2. Add 99 to both sides, with no flip for addition. Because the sign is ≥≥, the boundary is allowed. What is the smallest value xx can be?
Show the solution
Add 99 to both sides of x−9≥−2x−9≥−2 to get x≥7x≥7. Adding never flips the sign. The ≥≥ lets xx equal the boundary, so the smallest setting is 77​.
Practice
A garden permit allows at most 2828 liters, and each visit takes 88 liters, so over xx visits the rule is 8x≤288x≤28. Divide both sides by the positive 88, no flip. The word most means the boundary counts. What is the largest value xx can be? Give a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
Divide both sides of 8x≤288x≤28 by 88, a positive, so no flip. That gives x≤288=72x≤828​=27​, and at most means the boundary counts, so the largest is 7/27/2​. At x=72x=27​ the water used is exactly 2828 liters, right on the permit limit.
Practice
Cookie packs cost $7$7 each, and Priya wants to spend strictly more than $50$50 to clear a free-shipping bar, so 7x>507x>50. Solve it. The strict sign means 5050 itself does not count. What is the smallest integer number of packs she can buy?
Show the solution
Divide both sides of 7x>507x>50 by 77, a positive, so the sign stays put. That gives x>507x>750​, about 7.147.14, and the first whole number above it is 88​. Seven packs cost $49$49, which does not clear $50$50, so rounding down would miss the bar.
Practice
A deep-sea sensor's reading xx must satisfy −6x<30−6x<30. Divide both sides by −6−6 and flip the sign because the divisor is negative. What is the smallest integer xx can be?
Show the solution
Divide both sides of −6x<30−6x<30 by −6−6, and the negative divisor flips the sign, giving x>−5x>−5. The bound is strict, so −5−5 is out and the smallest integer allowed is −4−4​. Check it, −6⋅(−4)=24<30−6⋅(−4)=24<30 is true, while −6⋅(−5)=30<30−6⋅(−5)=30<30 is false.
Practice
A frost alarm trips whenever −5x>12−5x>12, where xx is a temperature that runs colder as it drops. Solve it, dividing by −5−5 and flipping the sign. What is the largest integer value xx can be?
Show the solution
Divide both sides of −5x>12−5x>12 by −5−5, and the negative divisor flips the sign, giving x<−125x<−512​, which is x<−2.4x<−2.4. Walking left from −2.4−2.4, the first integer is −3−3​. It is tempting to grab −2−2, but −2−2 is greater than −2.4−2.4, so it misses the bound.
Practice
A vending machine credits Mara once it counts more than 1919 tokens past a deposit, and xx cups give 4x−54x−5 such tokens, so she needs 4x−5>194x−5>19. Add 55, then divide by the positive 44, no flip. What is the smallest integer number of cups xx she can buy?
Show the solution
Add 55 to both sides of 4x−5>194x−5>19 to get 4x>244x>24, then divide by 44, a positive, so no flip. That gives x>6x>6, and since the bound is strict the smallest whole number is 77​. Six cups land on exactly 1919 tokens, which is not more than 1919.
Practice
A drone starts at a battery reading of 1010 and the lamp drains 44 per minute, so after xx minutes the reading is 10−4x10−4x, and the pilot keeps it on while 10−4x≥−610−4x≥−6. Subtract 1010, then divide by −4−4 and flip the sign. What is the largest value xx can be?
Show the solution
Subtract 1010 from both sides of 10−4x≥−610−4x≥−6 to get −4x≥−16−4x≥−16. Divide by −4−4, and the negative divisor flips ≥≥ into ≤≤, giving x≤4x≤4. The boundary is included, so the largest value is 44​. At x=4x=4 the reading is exactly −6−6, which the rule still allows, and at x=5x=5 it drops to −10−10.
Practice
One battery mode reads 7−x7−x and another reads 2x+12x+1 after xx minutes, and the first beats the second when 7−x>2x+17−x>2x+1. Gather the variable, then divide by a negative and flip the sign. What is the largest integer xx can be?
Show the solution
Subtract 2x2x from both sides of 7−x>2x+17−x>2x+1 to get 7−3x>17−3x>1, then subtract 77 to get −3x>−6−3x>−6. Divide by −3−3, which flips the sign, leaving x<2x<2. The bound is strict, so the largest integer is 11​. At x=2x=2 the two readings tie at 55, and a tie is not a win.
Practice
A batch of xx panels uses 3(x−2)3(x−2) ounces of grout because the first 22 panels are scrapped, and the bucket holds 1818 ounces, so 3(x−2)≤183(x−2)≤18. Distribute, then solve, dividing by the positive 33 with no flip. What is the largest value xx can be?
Show the solution
Distribute to get 3x−6≤183x−6≤18, add 66 for 3x≤243x≤24, then divide by 33, a positive, so no flip. That gives x≤8x≤8, and the bound is closed, so the largest is 88​. At x=8x=8 the grout used is 3(6)=183(6)=18 ounces, exactly the bucket, and x=9x=9 needs 2121.
Practice
A ferry logs every stop xx that is at least −5−5 and strictly west of 44, so −5≤x<4−5≤x<4. The left end is closed, so −5−5 counts, and the right end is open, so 44 does not. How many integer positions get logged?
Show the solution
Since −5−5 is included and 44 is not, the logged integers run −5,−4,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3−5,−4,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3. That is 99​ positions. Counting is faster as 3−(−5)=83−(−5)=8 steps plus one for the endpoint you started on.
Practice
A candle stands 3030 cm tall and burns down 2.52.5 cm each hour, so after hh hours its height is 30−2.5h30−2.5h, and it must stay at least 55 cm tall to sit in its holder, giving 30−2.5h≥530−2.5h≥5. Dividing by −2.5−2.5 flips the sign. What is the most whole hours the candle can burn?
Show the solution
Subtract 3030 from both sides of 30−2.5h≥530−2.5h≥5 to get −2.5h≥−25−2.5h≥−25. Divide by −2.5−2.5, and the negative divisor flips ≥≥ into ≤≤, giving h≤10h≤10. The boundary counts, so the candle can burn 1010​ whole hours. At 1010 hours it stands exactly 55 cm tall, which still sits in the holder, and at 1111 it is down to 2.52.5 cm.
